items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: Ed Berger and Vincent Pelote and I and some of the other people who worked for us would take turns doing the program.

ctx.x: It helped inform their choices of what to play, yeah, sure. It made them sound more informed.

And actually, one of the reasons why I did that, although I didn’t start initially, was that I’ve done quite a lot of radio over time. I started out at WBAI in New York. And Gunther Schuller and Martin Williams had a program called “The Scope of Jazz.” And Martin had to bow out and he turned it over to me. And so, that was back in the sixties. Nat Hentoff was also in it. Gunther was the first one and then he moved to Boston. Anyway, it was © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

like a series, one hour jazz, a Sunday night broadcast. But then once I got with the Institute we started, when WBGO was the new jazz radio station in Newark back thirty- some years ago, they came to us at the Institute and asked us to do a weekly program, and we decided to call it “Jazz from the Archives.” And so Ed Berger and Vincent Pelote and I and some of the other people who worked for us would take turns doing the program. items.title: Vincent Pelote interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 25, 2017
items.q: One of the first things I told Dan Morgenstern when I knew he was the Institute of Jazz Studies Director was, you know how many records I’ve bought strictly on the fact that you said it was a great record?

ctx.x: You know you’re in the record store and you’re reading and you learn who writes, who do you agree with, so I’m going to buy this because this person says this thing about it.

Yep. One of the first things I told Dan Morgenstern when I knew he was the Institute of Jazz Studies Director was, you know how many records I’ve bought strictly on the fact that you said it was a great record? And he gets all sheepish and everything.
Yeah, I was just going to say, “Well I hope you liked them.”

items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: In the music department, there was a young man who was a music major named Vincent Pelote, who had made himself available as a volunteer at the Institute... We got Vincent a scholarship to go to library school at Rutgers. He became a librarian... the three of us have been together for the whole stre

ctx.x: You were talking about traveling around and Jazz People, the book.

Going around, having this press agent, and doing television shows and radio. It was a big deal. That book did not become a best seller on account of that, but it went back into print in a paperback. It was a very handsome book. I didn’t like the cover, and neither did Ole, for that matter, but they – we had a much better one originally with just a clarinet with hands on it, but instead they put this cheesy picture of Benny Goodman and Red Norvo on it. Red had a big belly. It wasn’t very appealing. But that’s the…

They were consulting with me very kindly about “Jazz: the Personal Dimension.” Around that time I also, I think, met Ed Berger’s father, Morroe Berger.
